summary: A 1970 note proposing a language-machine for data reconfiguration, by three RAND authors. It deals with converting data from one arrangement to another so different systems can share it.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 83 proposes a Form Machine that converts data by applying ordered replacement rules. The authors also show how the rules could translate protocol commands between a console and the network.

how did early networks handle format differences
what is the form machine in rfc 83

subtitle: A syntax-driven Form Machine for converting data between formats.

tldr.problem: A protocol manager may need to convert data between different formats and interpret sequences of protocol messages.
tldr.mechanism: The proposed Form Machine applies an ordered set of replacement rules to input data, matching fields and emitting converted output.
tldr.outcome: The authors propose using the machine for data reconfiguration and for translating protocol commands, while explicitly saying it is not a general-purpose programming language.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 83 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC proposes a syntax-driven Form Machine and asks for comments on the language design.

sections.title: A Language for Data Reconfiguration
sections.content:
The note proposes a syntax-driven interpreter for converting data between formats, with examples of required conversions between RAND consoles and the UCLA Remote Job System on a 360/91. It also suggests using the Form Machine to simplify the Protocol Manager described in RFC 80.

The authors emphasize that the Form Machine is not intended to be a general-purpose programming language.
sections.plainLanguage: Different systems may need the same information in different formats. The proposed machine applies rules to change the data from one form to another.

sections.title: Forms, Rules and Terms
sections.content:
A form is an ordered set of replacement rules, from highest to lowest priority. The machine tries the current rule against the input; if it fails, it tries a lower-priority rule, and if it succeeds, it returns to the highest-priority rule for the next input.

A rule matches terms on its left side and emits terms on its right side. Terms can describe data types such as decimal, octal, hexadecimal, ASCII, EBCDIC or binary, along with values, lengths and repetition. The notation also supports variables, arithmetic expressions and references to previously matched terms.
sections.plainLanguage: A form is a ranked list of rules. Each rule looks for a pattern in the input and, when it matches, writes the corresponding output.

sections.title: Conversions and Output Handling
sections.content:
The note discusses limits and interpretations of terms, including how to handle arbitrary-length data and how to pad or truncate output. For character-to-character conversion, the output is left-justified and uses blank padding or truncation on the right. For numeric output, it is right-justified and uses zero padding or truncation on the left.

Examples show inserting literals, deleting fields, leaving space in an output buffer, handling arbitrary lengths, transposing fields, computing string length and compressing repeated symbols.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules can convert character and numeric data, insert or remove fields, and change field order. The note also gives rules for padding or shortening output when lengths differ.

sections.title: Using Forms in a Protocol Manager
sections.content:
The authors describe using forms to translate between console EBCDIC strings and network binary commands. They propose two system forms: one for console-to-network commands and a mirror form for network-to-console responses.

They also show how ordered rules and variables could represent protocol sequences, extract a socket number from a message and generate system calls. Some notation in these protocol examples is explicitly described as illustrative rather than part of the Form Machine language.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol manager could use one set of rules to turn console commands into network data and another to translate replies back. The authors give protocol examples but mark some of their notation as illustration only.
